strengths: Well-motivated identification of 'agreement bias' in MLLM verifiers with clear evidence of its prevalence across models, scales, and evaluation templates

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ~1,300 trajectories across multiple environments (VisualWebArena, OSWorld, robomimic), diverse models, extensive metrics, and both offline and online experiments
Practical and simple solution (SGV) that is easy to implement, requires no retraining, and shows consistent improvements (up to 25 pp in failure identification, 14 pp in accuracy)
Rigorous analysis ruling out alternative explanations with improved oracle evaluators achieving near-perfect human agreement and thorough qualitative examples
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation details, full prompts in appendices, and public release of code and updated VisualWebArena resources
Demonstrates practical impact beyond offline evaluation through online supervision and self-refinement applications with agents achieving new SOTA on benchmarks
Extensive ablation studies examining prior diversity, grounding tools, and first-step generation that provide insights into design choices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - SGV is conceptually straightforward (two-step prompting) and the core contribution is problem identification rather than a novel method
Incomplete mechanistic understanding of why agreement bias occurs and why conditioning on self-generated priors helps; attribution to 'knowledge extraction bottleneck' is somewhat superficial
Mixed calibration results showing Platt scaling provides minimal benefit and output distributions remain somewhat skewed, suggesting the underlying issue isn't fully resolved

Limited generalization evidence - evaluation is primarily on web/OS tasks with minimal robomimic results; unclear how well SGV transfers to other agent domains like robotics, games, or symbolic planning
Incomplete analysis of alternative bias mitigation approaches - ablations test SGV components but don't compare against qualitatively different solutions like ensembles or iterative refinement
Modest improvements in online supervision setting (2-3 pp gains) with absolute success rates remaining low, limiting practical impact on agent development workflows
Limited systematic analysis of failure modes - insufficient investigation of task types or agent behaviors where SGV provides minimal benefit or fails
Prior generation mechanism underspecified - what makes a good prior vs. poor one is not deeply analyzed, and design choices for specific prompt templates appear arbitrary
Quantitative comparison with human judgments is limited; claims about 'human-aligned evaluations' rely heavily on qualitative examples rather than systematic human evaluation
Paper is quite lengthy (54 pages) with redundancy between main text and appendices; key mechanistic insights could be developed more deeply
